label: PYQ-style
stem: State Henry's law. Why is the air in scuba divers' tanks diluted with helium?
model_answer:
**Henry's law:** at constant temperature the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution, $p=K_Hx$. [1]
Under high pressure at depth, more N$_2$ dissolves in blood. On coming up, pressure falls and N$_2$ comes out as bubbles that block capillaries (*bends*). Helium is much less soluble in blood, so air diluted with He avoids this. [1]

scheme.step: **Henry's law:** at constant temperature the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution, $p=K_Hx$.

Under high pressure at depth, more N$_2$ dissolves in blood. On coming up, pressure falls and N$_2$ comes out as bubbles that block capillaries (*bends*). Helium is much less soluble in blood, so air diluted with He avoids this.

hint: Gas solubility rises with pressure. Think about what happens as the diver comes back up.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why is osmotic pressure the preferred property for finding molar masses of proteins? What are isotonic solutions?
model_answer:
Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature (proteins denature on heating), uses molarity, and is large enough to measure even for very dilute solutions of high molar mass. [1]
**Isotonic solutions** have the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature, so no net osmosis occurs between them; e.g. 0.9% (m/V) NaCl and blood cell fluid. [1]

scheme.step: Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature (proteins denature on heating), uses molarity, and is large enough to measure even for very dilute solutions of high molar mass.
**Isotonic solutions** have the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature, so no net osmosis occurs between them; e.g. 0.9% (m/V) NaCl and blood cell fluid.

hint: Compare how big π is with how small ΔT would be for a dilute solution of a very large molecule.

label: PYQ-style
stem: 0.3 g of ethanoic acid ($M=60$ g mol$^{-1}$) dissolved in 30 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 0.45 K. Calculate the van't Hoff factor and the percentage association of the acid, if it forms a dimer. ($K_f$ of benzene = 5.12 K kg mol$^{-1}$)
model_answer:
Given: $w_2=0.3$ g, $w_1=30$ g, $M_2=60$, $\Delta T_f=0.45$ K.
$m=\dfrac{0.3\times1000}{60\times30}=0.1667$ mol kg$^{-1}$; $\Delta T_f(\text{calc})=K_fm=5.12\times0.1667=0.853$ K [1]
$i=\dfrac{\Delta T_f(\text{obs})}{\Delta T_f(\text{calc})}=\dfrac{0.45}{0.853}=\boxed{0.527}$ [1]
Dimer ($n=2$): $\alpha=\dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac12}=2(1-0.527)=0.945$ ⇒ **94.5% associated** [1]
hint: Find the expected ΔTf for i = 1 first; then i = observed ÷ expected. For a dimer, α = (1 − i)/(1 − ½).

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Calculate the boiling point of a solution of 10 g of CaCl$_2$ ($M=111$ g mol$^{-1}$) in 200 g of water, assuming complete dissociation. ($K_b$ = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$; b.p. of water 373.15 K) [3]
(b) Give reasons: (i) the elevation of boiling point of 1 M KCl is nearly double that of 1 M sugar solution; (ii) ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope. [2]
model_answer:
(a) $\ce{CaCl2 -> Ca^2+ + 2Cl-}$; complete dissociation ⇒ $i=3$ [½]
$m=\dfrac{10\times1000}{111\times200}=0.4505$ mol kg$^{-1}$ [1]
$\Delta T_b=iK_bm=3\times0.52\times0.4505=0.70$ K [1]
$T_b=373.15+0.70=\boxed{373.85\text{ K}}$ [½]
(b)(i) Colligative properties depend on the number of particles. KCl dissociates into two ions ($i\approx2$); sugar does not ($i=1$). [1]
(ii) The mixture shows positive deviation from Raoult's law (ethanol–water attractions are weaker than those in the pure liquids), so the total vapour pressure passes through a maximum and the boiling point through a minimum. [1]

scheme.step: (b)(i) Colligative properties depend on the number of particles. KCl dissociates into two ions ($i\approx2$); sugar does not ($i=1$).

(ii) The mixture shows positive deviation from Raoult's law (ethanol–water attractions are weaker than those in the pure liquids), so the total vapour pressure passes through a maximum and the boiling point through a minimum.

hint: CaCl₂ gives three ions, so i = 3. Molality needs kilograms of water.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Calculate the mole fraction of ethylene glycol ($\ce{C2H6O2}$) in a solution that is 25% ethylene glycol by mass.
model_answer:
**How much to write:** 4–5 lines (about 50 words) · 4 minutes. Write the formula first, then numbers; give the answer to three figures.

Take 100 g of solution: 25 g glycol, 75 g water. $n_\text{glycol}=\dfrac{25}{62}=0.403$ mol; $n_\text{water}=\dfrac{75}{18}=4.167$ mol **[1]**

$x_\text{glycol}=\dfrac{0.403}{0.403+4.167}=\boxed{0.088}$ (and $x_\text{water}=0.912$) **[1]**

**Where marks are lost:** Using 100 g of *water* instead of 100 g of solution; forgetting to say "take 100 g of solution"; no molar mass shown (62 g mol⁻¹).

scheme.step: Take 100 g of solution: 25 g glycol, 75 g water. $n_\text{glycol}=\dfrac{25}{62}=0.403$ mol; $n_\text{water}=\dfrac{75}{18}=4.167$ mol

hint: Assume 100 g of solution. Find moles of each component, then divide.

label: PYQ-style
stem: State Raoult's law for a solution of two volatile liquids. Show that it is a special case of Henry's law.
model_answer:
**How much to write:** 4–5 lines (about 50 words) · 4 minutes. One sentence of law + one equation; then the comparison in two lines.

The partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: $p_1=x_1p_1^\circ$, $p_2=x_2p_2^\circ$. **[1]**

Henry's law is $p=K_Hx$. Raoult's law has the same form with $K_H=p_1^\circ$; so Raoult's law is Henry's law with the constant equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component. **[1]**

**Where marks are lost:** Stating the law for a non-volatile solute instead of volatile liquids; writing the comparison in words without the two equations side by side.

scheme.step: The partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: $p_1=x_1p_1^\circ$, $p_2=x_2p_2^\circ$.
Henry's law is $p=K_Hx$. Raoult's law has the same form with $K_H=p_1^\circ$; so Raoult's law is Henry's law with the constant equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component.

hint: Write both laws as equations and compare the constants.

label: PYQ-style
stem: 1.00 g of a non-electrolyte solute dissolved in 50 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 0.40 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. ($K_f$ for benzene = 5.12 K kg mol$^{-1}$)
model_answer:
**How much to write:** 8–10 lines with every numerical step shown · 6 minutes.

Given: $w_2=1.00$ g, $w_1=50$ g, $\Delta T_f=0.40$ K, $K_f=5.12$ K kg mol$^{-1}$. To find: $M_2$. **[½]**

$\Delta T_f=K_f\,m=K_f\times\dfrac{w_2\times1000}{M_2\times w_1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $M_2=\dfrac{K_f\times w_2\times1000}{\Delta T_f\times w_1}$ **[1]**

$M_2=\dfrac{5.12\times1.00\times1000}{0.40\times50}$ **[1]**

$=\boxed{256\text{ g mol}^{-1}}$ **[½]**

**Where marks are lost:** No "given" line; missing unit on the answer (half a mark); using 50 g as kilograms without the factor 1000.
hint: Rearrange ΔTf = Kf·m for the molar mass, keeping the 1000 for grams.

label: PYQ-style
stem: The vapour pressure of pure water at 298 K is 23.8 mm Hg. 30 g of urea ($M=60$ g mol$^{-1}$) is dissolved in 846 g of water. Calculate the vapour pressure of water over this solution and its relative lowering.
model_answer:
**How much to write:** 8–10 lines with every numerical step shown · 6 minutes.

$n_\text{urea}=\dfrac{30}{60}=0.50$ mol; $n_\text{water}=\dfrac{846}{18}=47.0$ mol **[½]**

Raoult's law: $\dfrac{p^\circ-p}{p^\circ}=x_\text{urea}=\dfrac{0.50}{0.50+47.0}=0.0105$ **[1]**

Relative lowering $=\boxed{0.0105}$ (no unit) **[½]**

$p=p^\circ(1-x_\text{urea})=23.8\times(1-0.0105)=\boxed{23.55\text{ mm Hg}}$ **[1]**

**Where marks are lost:** Giving a unit to the relative lowering; using $x_	ext{water}$ in place of $x_	ext{urea}$; rounding too early (gives 23.5 or 23.6).
hint: Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) What is osmotic pressure? Why is it the preferred colligative property for finding the molar mass of proteins and polymers? Give two reasons. [2]
(b) 250 mL of an aqueous solution contains 1.50 g of a protein. Its osmotic pressure at 300 K is $3.00\times10^{-3}$ bar. Calculate the molar mass of the protein. ($R=0.083$ L bar mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) [3]
model_answer:
**How much to write:** about one page: part (a) in 6–8 lines, part (b) as a full numerical · 10–12 minutes.

(a) Osmotic pressure is the extra pressure that must be applied to a solution to just stop the flow of solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane. **[1]**

Reasons: it is measured at room temperature, so the protein is not denatured; and it gives a measurable value even for very dilute solutions of large molecules, whereas $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$ would be too small to measure. **[1]**

(b) Given: $w_2=1.50$ g, $V=0.250$ L, $\pi=3.00\times10^{-3}$ bar, $T=300$ K. $\pi=\dfrac{w_2RT}{M_2V}\Rightarrow M_2=\dfrac{w_2RT}{\pi V}$ **[1]**

$M_2=\dfrac{1.50\times0.083\times300}{3.00\times10^{-3}\times0.250}$ **[1]**

$=\boxed{4.98\times10^{4}\text{ g mol}^{-1}}$ **[1]**

**Where marks are lost:** Volume left in mL; one reason only in (a); writing "proteins are big" without saying why ΔT would be too small to measure.

scheme.step: (a) Osmotic pressure is the extra pressure that must be applied to a solution to just stop the flow of solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane.

Reasons: it is measured at room temperature, so the protein is not denatured; and it gives a measurable value even for very dilute solutions of large molecules, whereas $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$ would be too small to measure.
(b) Given: $w_2=1.50$ g, $V=0.250$ L, $\pi=3.00\times10^{-3}$ bar, $T=300$ K. $\pi=\dfrac{w_2RT}{M_2V}\Rightarrow M_2=\dfrac{w_2RT}{\pi V}$

hint: Convert 250 mL to litres before substituting into π = (w/M)RT/V.
